introduction: The first reading is a wonder more than a reproach: everyone has eyes and ears, and yet people are found not using them. The readings then follow heedlessness through its forms: conjecture taken for knowledge, a creation that speaks to no one, a long-awaited day that arrives unrecognized, names worshipped in place of what they name, a life spent on what passes, and a sleep that also overtakes believers. They end with how to help someone wake. Isaiah, the Gospels and the Qur’an say much of this in nearly the same words, and Plato’s cave, the Dhammapada’s “awake among the sleepers”, Blake, Pascal and Thoreau come at it from elsewhere. There are other accounts of the sleeper. Aristotle holds that all men by nature desire to know, and Mencius that human nature tends to good; Gray thinks it folly to disturb a bliss that rests on ignorance; Tennyson’s lotos-eaters ask to be let alone; Marx says that the dream is religion; and Khayyám cries Wake! on the way to the tavern.
questions: Bahá’u’lláh is “filled with wonder” that people do not use faculties they all possess, and Aristotle says that all men by nature desire to know. What, in these readings and their companions, comes between the faculty and its use?

“The abundance of bounty and blessing hath become the cause of heedlessness.” How can plenty make people inattentive? Compare Isaiah’s ox and ass, the nine lepers and Pascal’s remark about the chamber.

People awaited a promised day and did not know it when it came; two disciples walked beside the one they mourned. Why is what is expected so often unrecognized, and what do the readings ask of those who wait?

Marx calls religion the opium of the people, and these readings call the world asleep. Each claims to be the one awake. By what tests, offered in these passages, could a person tell waking from another dream?

Gray would leave the children their ignorance and the lotos-eaters ask to be let alone; God spares Nineveh because its people cannot tell their right hand from their left. How do the readings join severity about heedlessness with patience toward the heedless?
The warning “also addresses believers”. Which of these passages are spoken to people who think themselves awake, and what do they say is the sign of having fallen asleep again?

outside.why: “All men are endowed with the capacity to see and hear, yet we find them deprived of the privilege of using these faculties.” Proverbs names the gift whose neglect the reading wonders at: the hearing ear and the seeing eye, the Lord hath made even both of them.

The reading is “filled with wonder” that faculties given to all go unused. Jesus puts the same astonished questions to his own disciples in the boat: having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not?
“The abundance of bounty and blessing hath become the cause of heedlessness.” Isaiah opens with the fed animal that knows who feeds it, and the people who do not consider.

The faculty of recognition, says the reading, “hath remained undeveloped and hath, indeed, degenerated”. Aristotle begins his Metaphysics from the opposite observation: all men by nature desire to know. If he is right, what has become of the desire in the people the reading describes?
“They see the rising dust, but cannot perceive the swift-riding horseman.” Wordsworth’s Peter Bell sees a primrose by the river and nothing more.

“Mankind are naturally heedless and prone to commit injustice and excess.” Mencius held that human nature tends to good as water flows downward, and that only force makes it do otherwise. Which account of human beings do the other readings in this guide assume?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá cites Christ on those who “have eyes but see not, have ears but hear not”. The words are Isaiah’s commission, quoted in the Gospels, and they end as the reading’s quotation does, with healing.
“They form a conception and then worship that conception.” The psalm on idols says where that leads: eyes have they, but they see not; they that make them are like unto them.
“They have preferred conjecture to true knowledge and have contented themselves with doubt instead of certitude.” Plato’s prisoners take shadows for the truth and have never turned their heads.
“How many an ignorant one claimeth knowledge without proof.” Confucius defines knowledge by the admission such people will not make: when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it.
None has understood the root of the matter, “yet they speak whatsoever their idle fancies prompt them to speak”. Laozi: he who speaks does not know.
“The Most Great Ocean is manifest and visible before all faces, yet they remain bereft of it.” John’s prologue: the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.

“The very rocks have testified to the Lord of all being, yet the people remain behind a mighty veil.” Asked to silence his disciples, Jesus answers that if these held their peace the stones would cry out.
The Nightingale has warbled and the Spirit cried out, “yet the people remain sunk in slumber”. Jesus likens his generation to children in the market: we have piped unto you, and ye have not danced.
“This is a Day wherein all things proclaim.” The psalmist hears such proclamation daily, day unto day uttering speech, in a voice that is not heard as speech.

“The birds warble, seized by the rapture of the Manifestation, yet the people perceive not.” Hopkins, sure that the world is charged with grandeur, asks the same question: why do men then now not reck his rod?
“The veils have covered their sight.” The Qur’an locates the blindness: it is not the eyes that grow blind, but the hearts within the bosoms.
“The fragrances of divine revelation have permeated the world, yet the servants remain heedless.” The Qur’an: how many a portent in the heavens and the earth they pass by with face averted!

Verses descend like rain, and the reading asks “what hath befallen the people that their ears are barred”. The fifty-third chapter of Isaiah begins with that bewilderment: who hath believed our report?

Sight and hearing are given to all, yet “they are not employed in their proper place”. Blake: if the doors of perception were cleansed every thing would appear to man as it is, infinite; man has closed himself up.

If sovereignty meant “earthly sovereignty and worldly dominion”, the reading argues, it would not be true of God Himself, most of whose creatures disobey Him. Jesus before Pilate: my kingdom is not of this world.
What the Books promised has appeared, “and yet the people, though they look upon them, comprehend them not”. Two disciples walk seven miles beside the one they are mourning, and do not know him.
“All awaited the days of attainment, yet when the Self-Sufficient … appeared, they turned away.” John the Baptist says to a waiting people: there standeth one among you, whom ye know not.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that expectation was fixed “on the text of Isaiah” read literally. John’s Gospel records the argument from the text as it was made at the time: shall Christ come out of Galilee?
“They deny that whereby they pride themselves above all the peoples of the earth.” Jesus to those who search the scriptures: they are they which testify of me, and ye will not come to me.
“All people were awaiting the days of God, yet when the Sun of Revelation shone forth … all were heedless.” Jesus weeps over the city: thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.
Pharaoh’s people “regarded the teachings and the law of Moses as mere fancy”. Paul meets it in his own day: Christ crucified is unto the Greeks foolishness.
“On the day of the establishment of the Kingdom, they remain heedless and negligent.” Jesus compares it to the days of Noah: they ate, they drank, they married, until the flood came.
The reading’s purpose is to show “how unobservant are the people of the world”. Jesus tells those who ask when the kingdom will come that it does not come with observation.
At each Manifestation “the people were heedless … except for a few who investigated”. The Sermon on the Mount expects the same proportion: strait is the gate, and few there be that find it.
Mankind is seen “worshipping names” and courting danger “in the mere hope of perpetuating their names”. Gray, among graves without names: the paths of glory lead but to the grave.

“After death one’s name shall avail him nothing.” Shakespeare promises a friend the contrary, that he will outlive marble in a poem. Four centuries on, the poem is read and no one is sure of the friend’s name. Whose side does that take?
“They make mention of God throughout the night and day, yet when He appears in truth they deny Him.” Jesus: not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter.

Having seen power and bounty, “they pass it by and occupy themselves with matters unworthy of mention”. Pascal traced all the unhappiness of men to one fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
“Has not the time come for those who sleep to awaken?” The Qur’an asks it in nearly the same words of believers whose hearts have hardened with the passing of time.

“Do they think they shall not depart, shall not enter the graves?” Gray, watching schoolboys at play, would not tell them: where ignorance is bliss, ’tis folly to be wise. Is there a kindness in letting people sleep, and what would the reading say to it?
“Others, having forsaken the river of eternal life, content themselves with a vanishing drop.” Jeremiah: they have forsaken the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out broken cisterns.
“Being overcome by the drunkenness of corrupt inclinations, the people of the earth find themselves in a state of stupor.” The Qur’an: hast thou seen him who maketh his desire his god?
The heedless life ends “with no trace, no leaves, no blossom and no fruit”. Jeremiah has the lament of people who discover it: the harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved.

“Like tiny worms in the depths of the earth they strive to make a nest and dwelling, while one flood will destroy” it. James to the planners of next year’s trade: ye know not what shall be on the morrow.

“The mass of the people are occupied with self and worldly desire … captives of the world of nature.” Hamlet: what is a man, if his chief good and market of his time be but to sleep and feed? A beast, no more.
If a soul becomes heedless, “the treasures and riches of the earth shall profit him not”. The Gospel’s question: what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
“With your lips ye profess the one true faith of God … ye walk on My earth complacent and self-satisfied.” The letter to Laodicea is addressed to believers too: neither cold nor hot.
The reading speaks to the complacent, “heedless that My earth is weary of you”. Amos: woe to them that are at ease in Zion.
“The fire of love became extinguished and beauty’s attraction became veiled.” To the church at Ephesus: thou hast left thy first love; remember from whence thou art fallen.
Some undermine the Cause “counting themselves among the mature and perfect ones”. Paul: let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.

Those who have had “healing counsels and conclusive admonitions” are found “more heedless than all who dwell on earth”. Jesus weighs heedlessness by what one was given: unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required. Why does the reading speak most severely to those nearest?

A land once “a lamp, streaming with the rays of Divine knowledge” is eclipsed by “the idleness and lethargy of her people”. Tagore’s prayer for India, written in the same generation: into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake.

“How heedless and ignorant are the people of the world! How gross the darkness which envelops them!” God’s last word to Jonah about Nineveh describes the same people, who cannot discern between their right hand and their left, as a reason to spare them. Does the reading’s exclamation leave room for that pity?

Despite afflictions, “all remain captive to the sleep of negligence … neither prayer nor supplication”. In the storm the heathen shipmaster finds the prophet asleep below: what meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God.

The heedless “fondly imagine that massacre and crucifixion cause the fire of the Word of God to be extinguished”. Tertullian corrected the magistrates of Rome on the point: the blood of Christians is seed.
People “have not been awakened by the great cry and supreme calamities”. The Qur’an says of some hearers: whether thou warn them or warn them not, it is alike for them.

An eye of justice “would instantly proclaim” belief, but “eyes are afflicted with the soreness of vain imaginings”. Bacon found the same soreness in every mind, his own included: what a man had rather were true he more readily believes. How would a reader apply his rule to himself?
The Wronged One “called out with His loudest voice” to rulers, divines and philosophers. Wisdom in Proverbs stands at the gates and in the high places: unto you, O men, I call.
Most Iranians remain asleep, though “the divine call was raised from that land”. Jesus at Nazareth: no prophet is accepted in his own country.
“The master of the house has come to the door, but the household has barred it.” The Apocalypse has the same figure, with the door still shut: behold, I stand at the door, and knock.

The household says, “We are content in this abasement and find rest in this disorder.” Tennyson gives the contented their own song, and it is a beautiful one: let us alone. What does the reading owe to people who say that sincerely?
“The peoples of the world are fast asleep.” Thoreau counted one in a hundred million awake to a poetic or divine life: to be awake is to be alive.
Were they to wake, “they would cast away everything they possess … that their Lord may remember them”. The man in the parable does it for joy: he sells all that he has and buys the field.

The reading calls the peoples of the world asleep and drunk with desire. Marx called religion itself the opium of the people, the sleep from which they must be roused. Each sees the other’s waking as a dream. What would settle it?
“Most men are this day accounted as sucklings … their days of weaning have not yet come.” The Epistle to the Hebrews says it to its readers: ye have need of milk, and not of strong meat.

“All the heavenly Scriptures of the past attest to the greatness of this Day … Yet despite all this the people have remained heedless.” The reproach on the Emmaus road: slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken.

“Whoso hath in bygone ages asked Us to produce the signs of God, hath, no sooner had We revealed them to him, repudiated.” Jesus refuses the request for a sign from heaven, to people who can read the weather.
“The poison of heedlessness hath affected all limbs”, and some are “healed with the Supreme Medicine”. Jesus: they that be whole need not a physician.
“The eyes see it not, the ears are deaf, and the hearts and minds are oblivious.” The Qur’an lists the same three, hearts, eyes and ears, and gives such people their name: these are the neglectful.
“With every passing day, these signs will be revealed … But alas! The people of Persia remain wrapt in heedless slumber.” Paul: now it is high time to awake out of sleep; the night is far spent.
“Man is not grateful for this supreme good, but sleeps the sleep of negligence.” Ten are healed and one comes back: where are the nine?
“Thou didst recognize My Revelation when men of renown were immersed in manifest idle fancies.” Paul to the church at Corinth: not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble are called.

The reading speaks of “remedies that purify and tranquillize and soothe”, given to deliver the world from heedlessness. Socrates offered Athens one remedy, daily examination of oneself and others, and was put to death for it. Is his remedy among those the reading means?
“This is everlasting regret and this is endless loss.” Marley’s ghost has that regret: mankind was my business.
“They have sold this brilliant crown for a mere trifle.” The Gospel names the price of the best known of such sales.
The witless say “that the Day of the Lord hath passed and darkness hath encompassed all”. Emerson charged the churches of his day with the same assumption: they speak as if God were dead.
Some make their dwelling in the lowest depths: “these are as the cattle.” The psalm: man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish.
“They will awaken when the caravan has reached its destination.” Jesus tells of ten who waited with lamps, and five with no oil when the hour came.
“Such Divine Music was played for them, but they did not listen to it.” Ezekiel’s hearers do listen, as to one with a pleasant voice, and do nothing.
“It has always been the practice of the heedless to hold back the sincere ones.” Jesus: ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in.
When the veil was removed, “all turned away their faces, closed their eyes, fell asleep”. In Gethsemane the three closest disciples do it: what, could ye not watch with me one hour?
“Yet another group remained in the sleep of heedlessness, lying upon the bed of error.” Proverbs: how long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?
“They cling to graves and are heedless of resurrection.” The women at the tomb are asked: why seek ye the living among the dead?
Some imagine that, the Sun having set from its human temple, “darkness has been established upon the throne”. Shelley, mourning Keats: Heaven’s light forever shines, Earth’s shadows fly.
“The world is heedless—be ye aware. All are asleep—be ye wakeful.” The Dhammapada: earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers, the wise man advances like a racer.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks his friends to be the exception. Paul asks it of the Thessalonians: let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober.

“All are asleep—be ye wakeful.” FitzGerald’s Khayyám begins with the same cry, Wake! and goes on to the tavern door, since the flower that once has blown for ever dies. Awake to what? The readings and the poem give different answers.
Some imagine “that the doors of heavenly bounties are closed, that the rain of great mercy hath been cut off”. The Qur’an answers an old form of that thought: nay, both His hands are spread out wide.
Those who turned toward the Cause “broke the chains of imitation”. Kant called such chains self-incurred, and gave the age its motto: have courage to use your own reason.

“Arise in My Name, then speak forth My praise amidst them that are heedless.” Socrates describes his own calling to the Athenians: a gadfly given to the state by God, arousing and persuading and reproaching.
The slumbering “became heedless of that for which they were created”. The Qur’an: deemed ye then that We had created you for naught?
Intoxicated by desire, they forgot their purpose. The Qur’an describes a forgetting that returns on the forgetter: they forgot Allah, therefore He caused them to forget their souls.
“The Cry hath been raised, yet they slumber; nay, they are as the dead.” The Dhammapada: those who are in earnest do not die; those who are thoughtless are as if dead already.
“The eyes of the world have been afflicted with the ophthalmia of vain imaginings.” In John the worst of the disease is not knowing one has it: now ye say, We see.
“Praise thou God that … thou hast been awakened, hast been made aware.” Jacob wakes at Bethel: surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not.
All others are “slumbering, heedless and unaware”. The prodigal’s turning begins with four words: he came to himself.

She “mayest glory over all other maidens”, having been delivered “by the hand of divine favor”. Paul asks the awakened what makes them differ, and what they have that they did not receive. How do the reading’s two phrases already answer him?
“No punishment hath been or shall be greater than heedlessness.” Mencius finds it lamentable in the same way: people look for a lost fowl or dog, and lose their own mind and do not know to seek it.
“Be not grieved by the opposition of people and their turning away.” The Qur’an comforts its Prophet in the same words: let not thy soul expire in sighings for them.

The opposers “are weak and immature” and “must be educated with the waters of divine wisdom”. Paul tells the Athenians that God overlooked the times of ignorance, and now calls everyone. How does one hold the patience and the summons together?
“The souls of men are ravening wolves.” Hobbes thought both sayings true, that man to man is a kind of God, and that man to man is an arrant wolf.
“Rely upon God … For the people are wandering in the paths of delusion.” The Qur’an relieves even its Prophet of the result: thou guidest not whom thou lovest, but Allah guideth whom He will.

“Pay no heed to the peoples of the world, for that which their mouths utter is like unto the droning of a gnat.” Paul: with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man’s judgment.
“In reality the people are the cause of the rejection of these divines.” Jeremiah has the same reversal in a clause: the priests bear rule, and my people love to have it so.

revelation-stand-at-the-door.text: Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me

isaiah-ox-knoweth-his-owner.text: The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider

mark-having-eyes-see-ye-not.text: perceive ye not yet, neither understand? have ye your heart yet hardened? Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember

romans-high-time-to-awake.text: And that, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed. The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light

thessalonians-let-us-not-sleep.text: Ye are all the children of light, and the children of the day: we are not of the night, nor of darkness. Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober

proverbs-sluggard.text: How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man

luke-days-of-noe.text: And as it was in the days of Noe, so shall it be also in the days of the Son of man. They did eat, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ark, and the flood came, and destroyed them all

matthew-made-light-of-it.text: The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king, which made a marriage for his son, And sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden to the wedding: and they would not come. Again, he sent forth other servants, saying, Tell them which are bidden, Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage. But they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise

matthew-watch-one-hour.text: And he cometh unto the disciples, and findeth them asleep, and saith unto Peter, What, could ye not watch with me one hour

hosea-lack-of-knowledge.text: My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge

psalm-eyes-have-they.text: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands. They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not: They have ears, but they hear not: noses have they, but they smell not: They have hands, but they handle not: feet have they, but they walk not: neither speak they through their throat. They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them

psalm-beasts-that-perish.text: Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish

john-loved-darkness.text: And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil

john-darkness-comprehended-it-not.text: In him was life; and the life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not

luke-stones-would-cry-out.text: And some of the Pharisees from among the multitude said unto him, Master, rebuke thy disciples. And he answered and said unto them, I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out

deuteronomy-consider-their-latter-end.text: For they are a nation void of counsel, neither is there any understanding in them. O that they were wise, that they understood this, that they would consider their latter end

jeremiah-stork-knoweth.text: Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; and the turtle and the crane and the swallow observe the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of the Lord

jeremiah-harvest-is-past.text: The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved

matthew-piped-and-not-danced.text: But whereunto shall I liken this generation? It is like unto children sitting in the markets, and calling unto their fellows, And saying, We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned unto you, and ye have not lamented

jonah-o-sleeper.text: But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep. So the shipmaster came to him, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not

amos-at-ease-in-zion.text: Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria

genesis-i-knew-it-not.text: And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not. And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven

luke-eyes-were-holden.text: And it came to pass, that, while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them. But their eyes were holden that they should not know him

john-whom-ye-know-not.text: John answered them, saying, I baptize with water: but there standeth one among you, whom ye know not

isaiah-who-hath-believed.text: Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed

proverbs-hearing-ear.text: The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, the Lord hath made even both of them

luke-came-to-himself.text: And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee

acts-times-of-ignorance.text: And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent

luke-few-stripes.text: And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes. But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more

mark-watch.text: Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning: Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping. And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch

luke-excuses.text: And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused. And another said, I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to prove them: I pray thee have me excused. And another said, I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come

quran-as-the-cattle.text: Already have We urged unto hell many of the jinn and humankind, having hearts wherewith they understand not, and having eyes wherewith they see not, and having ears wherewith they hear not. These are as the cattle - nay, but they are worse! These are the neglectful.

quran-hearts-grow-blind.text: Have they not travelled in the land, and have they hearts wherewith to feel and ears wherewith to hear? For indeed it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts, which are within the bosoms, that grow blind.

quran-deaf-dumb-blind.text: Deaf, dumb and blind; and they return not.

quran-reckoning-draweth-nigh.text: Their reckoning draweth nigh for mankind, while they turn away in heedlessness.

quran-appearance-of-the-life-of-the-worl.text: They know only some appearance of the life of the world, and are heedless of the Hereafter.

quran-forgot-their-souls.text: And be not ye as those who forgot Allah, therefor He caused them to forget their souls. Such are the evil-doers.

quran-pass-by-with-face-averted.text: How many a portent is there in the heavens and the earth which they pass by with face averted!

quran-alike-whether-thou-warn.text: Whether thou warn them or thou warn them not, it is alike for them, for they believe not.

quran-removed-thy-covering.text: (And unto the evil-doer it is said): Thou wast in heedlessness of this. Now We have removed from thee thy covering, and piercing is thy sight this day.

quran-desire-to-be-his-god.text: Hast thou seen him who maketh his desire his god, and Allah sendeth him astray purposely, and sealeth up his hearing and his heart, and setteth on his sight a covering? Then who will lead him after Allah (hath condemned him)? Will ye not then heed?

quran-created-for-naught.text: Deemed ye then that We had created you for naught, and that ye would not be returned unto Us?

quran-expire-in-sighings.text: Is he, the evil of whose deeds is made fairseeming unto him so that he deemeth it good, (other than Satan's dupe)? Allah verily sendeth whom He will astray, and guideth whom He will; so let not thy soul expire in sighings for them. Lo! Allah is Aware of what they do!

quran-rivalry-in-increase.text: Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you

dhammapada-awake-among-the-sleepers.text: Earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers, the wise man advances like a racer, leaving behind the hack

dhammapada-earnestness.text: Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvana), thoughtlessness the path of death. Those who are in earnest do not die, those who are thoughtless are as if dead already

mencius-lost-mind.text: When men's fowls and dogs are lost, they know to seek for them again, but they lose their mind, and do not know to seek for it
mencius-lost-mind.author: Mencius

shakespeare-sleep-and-feed.text: What is a man, / If his chief good and market of his time / Be but to sleep and feed? a beast, no more. / Sure, he that made us with such large discourse, / Looking before and after, gave us not / That capability and god-like reason / To fust in us unused
shakespeare-sleep-and-feed.author: William Shakespeare

pascal-own-chamber.text: I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber
pascal-own-chamber.author: Blaise Pascal

khayyam-wake.text: WAKE! For the Sun, who scatter'd into flight / The Stars before him from the Field of Night, / Drives Night along with them from Heav'n, and strikes / The Sultan's Turret with a Shaft of Light
khayyam-wake.author: Omar Khayyám

maimonides-wake-up-sleepers.text: Wake up you sleepy ones from your sleep and you who slumber, arise. Inspect your deeds, repent, remember your Creator
maimonides-wake-up-sleepers.author: Moses Maimonides

plato-unexamined-life.text: the greatest good of man is daily to converse about virtue, and all that concerning which you hear me examining myself and others, and that the life which is unexamined is not worth living
plato-unexamined-life.author: Plato

thoreau-only-that-day-dawns.text: The light which puts out our eyes is darkness to us. Only that day dawns to which we are awake. There is more day to dawn. The sun is but a morning star
thoreau-only-that-day-dawns.author: Henry David Thoreau

tennyson-let-us-alone.text: Let us alone. What pleasure can we have / To war with evil? Is there any peace / In ever climbing up the climbing wave?
tennyson-let-us-alone.author: Alfred Tennyson

gray-ignorance-is-bliss.text: Thought would destroy their Paradise. / No more;—where ignorance is bliss, / 'Tis folly to be wise
gray-ignorance-is-bliss.author: Thomas Gray
gray-ignorance-is-bliss.work: Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College
